claim: PDE2A2-GFP is distinctly located at the mitochondria in primary neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVM).
source: When we expressed PDE2A2-GFP in primary neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVM), we found that it is distinctly located at the mitochondria, unlike PDE2A1-GFP, which is cytosolic, and PDE2A3-GFP, which localises predominantly to the plasmalemma (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data showing colocalization with mitochondrial markers in Figure 1A.

claim: PDE2A1-GFP is cytosolic in NRVM.
source: When we expressed PDE2A2-GFP in primary neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVM), we found that it is distinctly located at the mitochondria, unlike PDE2A1-GFP, which is cytosolic, and PDE2A3-GFP, which localises predominantly to the plasmalemma (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 1A showing cytosolic distribution.

claim: PDE2A3-GFP localises predominantly to the plasmalemma in NRVM.
source: When we expressed PDE2A2-GFP in primary neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVM), we found that it is distinctly located at the mitochondria, unlike PDE2A1-GFP, which is cytosolic, and PDE2A3-GFP, which localises predominantly to the plasmalemma (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 1A showing plasma membrane localization.

claim: Expression of PDE2A2wt-RFP results in more fragmented mitochondria compared to expression of its catalytically inactive variant PDE2A2dn-RFP.
source: We also observed that expression of PDE2A2wt-RFP results in more fragmented mitochondria compared to expression of its catalytically inactive variant PDE2A2dn-RFP (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 1B showing differences in mitochondrial morphology.

claim: Treatment of NRVM with the selective PDE2A inhibitor Bay 60-7550 (1 µM) results in significant mitochondrial elongation compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: To further investigate whether PDE2A2 has a role in the modulation of mitochondria morphology, we treated NRVM with the selective PDE2A inhibitor Bay 60–7550 (1 µM) and found significant mitochondrial elongation compared to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing quantitative analysis of mitochondrial length in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Selective inhibition of PDE3 with cilostamide (10 µM) has no effect on mitochondrial morphology in NRVM.
source: Increasing cAMP levels via selective inhibition of PDE3 with cilostamide (10 µM) had no effect (Figure 1C,D), whereas maximal elevation of cAMP, as achieved by application of the tmAC activator forskolin (25 µM) and the non-selective PDE inhibitor isobutyl-methyl-xanthine (IBMX, 100 µM), also resulted in mitochondria elongation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C,D showing no change in mitochondrial length with cilostamide treatment.

claim: Maximal elevation of cAMP by application of forskolin (25 µM) and IBMX (100 µM) results in mitochondria elongation in NRVM.
source: Increasing cAMP levels via selective inhibition of PDE3 with cilostamide (10 µM) had no effect (Figure 1C,D), whereas maximal elevation of cAMP, as achieved by application of the tmAC activator forskolin (25 µM) and the non-selective PDE inhibitor isobutyl-methyl-xanthine (IBMX, 100 µM), also resulted in mitochondria elongation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C,D showing increased mitochondrial length.

claim: Knock down of PDE2A expression in NRVM using siPDE2 results in elongated mitochondria.
source: Knock down of PDE2A expression in NRVM, using the small interfering RNA sequence siPDE2 (Stangherlin et al., 2011), also resulted in elongated mitochondria (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1E showing increased mitochondrial length after siRNA knockdown, with citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of a siRNA-resistant PDE2A2wt-GFP rescues the mitochondrial phenotype caused by PDE2A knockdown.
source: The specificity of the siRNA effect was confirmed by rescue of the mitochondrial phenotype upon overexpression of a siRNA-resistant PDE2A2wt-GFP (Zoccarato et al., 2015) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1E showing rescue of mitochondrial morphology, with citation to previous work.

claim: Treatment of H9C2 cells with Bay 60-7550 results in more elongated mitochondria.
source: In line with the above findings, treatment of the myoblast cell line H9C2 with Bay 60–7550 resulted in more elongated mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas expression of PDE2A2wt-GFP, but not expression of PDE4D7wt-GFP, resulted in mitochondria fragmentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of PDE2A2wt-GFP, but not PDE4D7wt-GFP, results in mitochondria fragmentation in H9C2 cells.
source: In line with the above findings, treatment of the myoblast cell line H9C2 with Bay 60–7550 resulted in more elongated mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas expression of PDE2A2wt-GFP, but not expression of PDE4D7wt-GFP, resulted in mitochondria fragmentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing differential effects of PDE2A2 vs PDE4D7.

claim: Treatment of NRVM lysates with Bay 60-7550 shows significant increase in Drp1 phosphorylation at the PKA site ser637.
source: Western blotting analysis of lysates from NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 showed significant increase in Drp1 phosphorylation at the PKA site ser637 (Figure 1F,G) compared to DMSO-treated controls, whereas no increased phosphorylation was detected at ser616, a site phosphorylated by the kinase CDK1 (Taguchi et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F,G showing increased phospho-Drp1 (ser637).

claim: Bay 60-7550 treatment does not increase Drp1 phosphorylation at ser616 in NRVM.
source: Western blotting analysis of lysates from NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 showed significant increase in Drp1 phosphorylation at the PKA site ser637 (Figure 1F,G) compared to DMSO-treated controls, whereas no increased phosphorylation was detected at ser616, a site phosphorylated by the kinase CDK1 (Taguchi et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing no change in phospho-Drp1 (ser616), with citation to previous work on CDK1.

claim: Ser616 on Drp1 is phosphorylated by the kinase CDK1.
source: Western blotting analysis of lysates from NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 showed significant increase in Drp1 phosphorylation at the PKA site ser637 (Figure 1F,G) compared to DMSO-treated controls, whereas no increased phosphorylation was detected at ser616, a site phosphorylated by the kinase CDK1 (Taguchi et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taguchi et al., 2007.

claim: Bay 60-7550 treatment has no effect on mitochondrial morphology in mouse embryonic fibroblasts in which DRP1 was genetically ablated (MEFsDRP1-/-).
source: No effect of Bay 60–7550 treatment on mitochondrial morphology was found in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) in which DRP1 was genetically ablated (Ishihara et al., 2009) (MEFsDRP1-/-) (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing no change in mitochondrial morphology in DRP1 knockout cells, with citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of wild type Drp1 (Drp1 wtGFP) in MEFsDRP1-/- rescues the effect of Bay 60-7550 treatment on mitochondrial morphology.
source: Expression of wild type Drp1 (Drp1 wtGFP) in MEFsDRP1-/-, but not of a DRP1 mutant that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA (Drp1 Mut-GFP), rescued the effect of Bay 60–7550 treatment (Figure 1H), confirming that elongation of mitochondria on inhibition of PDE2A is mediated by PKA phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing rescue of mitochondrial elongation response.

claim: Expression of a DRP1 mutant that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA (Drp1 Mut-GFP) does not rescue the effect of Bay 60-7550 treatment in MEFsDRP1-/-.
source: Expression of wild type Drp1 (Drp1 wtGFP) in MEFsDRP1-/-, but not of a DRP1 mutant that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA (Drp1 Mut-GFP), rescued the effect of Bay 60–7550 treatment (Figure 1H), confirming that elongation of mitochondria on inhibition of PDE2A is mediated by PKA phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing lack of rescue with phosphorylation-deficient mutant.

claim: Elongation of mitochondria on inhibition of PDE2A is mediated by PKA phosphorylation of Drp1.
source: Expression of wild type Drp1 (Drp1 wtGFP) in MEFsDRP1-/-, but not of a DRP1 mutant that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA (Drp1 Mut-GFP), rescued the effect of Bay 60–7550 treatment (Figure 1H), confirming that elongation of mitochondria on inhibition of PDE2A is mediated by PKA phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing differential rescue by wild-type vs phosphorylation-deficient Drp1.

claim: MEFsPDE2KO have significantly more elongated mitochondria than the wild type counterpart (MEFswt).
source: Figure 2A,C shows that MEFsPDE2KO have significantly more elongated mitochondria than the wild type counterpart (MEFswt).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2A,C showing quantitative analysis of mitochondrial length.

claim: The MEFsPDE2KO mitochondrial phenotype can be completely rescued by expression of PDE2A2wt-RFP.
source: The MEFsPDE2KO mitochondrial phenotype could be completely rescued by expression of a red fluorescent protein (RFP)-tagged PDE2A2 (PDE2A2wt-RFP), whereas expression of a catalytically inactive mutant of PDE2A2 (PDE2A2dn-RFP) in MEFsWT resulted in elongated mitochondria (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B,C showing rescue of mitochondrial morphology.

claim: Expression of catalytically inactive PDE2A2 (PDE2A2dn-RFP) in MEFsWT results in elongated mitochondria.
source: The MEFsPDE2KO mitochondrial phenotype could be completely rescued by expression of a red fluorescent protein (RFP)-tagged PDE2A2 (PDE2A2wt-RFP), whereas expression of a catalytically inactive mutant of PDE2A2 (PDE2A2dn-RFP) in MEFsWT resulted in elongated mitochondria (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B,C showing mitochondrial elongation.

claim: Both PDE2A2wt-RFP and PDE2A2dn-RFP localise to mitochondria with no appreciable cytosolic localisation.
source: It should be noted that both PDE2A2wt-RFP and PDE2A2dn-RFP localise to mitochondria with no appreciable cytosolic localisation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 2B showing mitochondrial localization.

claim: The rescue effect of PDE2A2wt-RFP in MEFsPDE2KO is the consequence of local cAMP hydrolysis at the organelle.
source: This suggests that the rescue effect of PDE2A2wt-RFP in MEFsPDE2KO is the consequence of local cAMP hydrolysis at the organelle, and that elongation of mitochondria in MEFsWT expressing PDE2A2dn-RFP relies on a local increase in cAMP following displacement of the endogenous active mitochondrial PDE2A2 (Stangherlin et al., 2011; Zoccarato et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that catalytically active PDE2A2 rescues the phenotype while inactive PDE2A2 causes elongation, with citations to previous work.

claim: Elongation of mitochondria in MEFsWT expressing PDE2A2dn-RFP relies on a local increase in cAMP following displacement of the endogenous active mitochondrial PDE2A2.
source: This suggests that the rescue effect of PDE2A2wt-RFP in MEFsPDE2KO is the consequence of local cAMP hydrolysis at the organelle, and that elongation of mitochondria in MEFsWT expressing PDE2A2dn-RFP relies on a local increase in cAMP following displacement of the endogenous active mitochondrial PDE2A2 (Stangherlin et al., 2011; Zoccarato et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inactive PDE2A2 causes elongation, likely by displacing active enzyme, with citations to previous work.

claim: MEFsPDE2KO cells treated with the PKA inhibitor H89 show complete reversal of the mitochondrial phenotype.
source: MEFsPDE2KO cells treated with the PKA inhibitor H89 show complete reversal of the mitochondrial phenotype, confirming involvement of PKA downstream of PDE2A inhibition (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2D showing reversal of mitochondrial elongation with PKA inhibitor.

claim: PKA is involved downstream of PDE2A inhibition in regulating mitochondrial morphology.
source: MEFsPDE2KO cells treated with the PKA inhibitor H89 show complete reversal of the mitochondrial phenotype, confirming involvement of PKA downstream of PDE2A inhibition (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2D showing that PKA inhibition reverses the phenotype.

claim: PDE2A2 has been previously reported to be found in the mitochondrial matrix where it hydrolyses cAMP generated locally by sAC.
source: It has been previously reported that PDE2A2 is found in the mitochondrial matrix, where it hydrolyses cAMP generated locally by sAC (Acin-Perez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Acin-Perez et al., 2011.

claim: The molecular machinery that regulates mitochondria fission/fusion, including Drp1, is not localised to the matrix.
source: However, the molecular machinery that regulates mitochondria fission/fusion, including Drp1, is not localised to the matrix and any cAMP generated in the matrix cannot escape this compartment as the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) is impermeable to it (Di Benedetto et al., 2008; Acin-Perez et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Benedetto et al., 2008 and Acin-Perez et al., 2009.

claim: The inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) is impermeable to cAMP.
source: However, the molecular machinery that regulates mitochondria fission/fusion, including Drp1, is not localised to the matrix and any cAMP generated in the matrix cannot escape this compartment as the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) is impermeable to it (Di Benedetto et al., 2008; Acin-Perez et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Benedetto et al., 2008 and Acin-Perez et al., 2009.

claim: Inhibition of PDE2A generates a similar elevation of cAMP in the bulk cytosol as inhibition of PDE3 in NRVM.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, inhibition of PDE2A generates a similar elevation of cAMP in the bulk cytosol as inhibition of PDE3.
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3A showing comparable cAMP increases.

claim: A significantly higher increase in cAMP is detected at the OMM upon inhibition of PDE2A compared to inhibition of PDE3 in NRVM.
source: In contrast, and in line with the effect on mitochondria morphology (Figure 1C,D), a significantly higher increase in cAMP was detected at the OMM upon inhibition of PDE2A, as compared to inhibition of PDE3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3B showing differential cAMP increases at the OMM.

claim: Bay 60-7550 does not increase cAMP levels in the mitochondrial matrix in NRVM.
source: Surprisingly, Bay 60–7550 did not increase cAMP levels in the matrix (Figure 3C) and was unable to appreciably increase in the matrix the concentration of the membrane permeable cAMP analogue 8-CPT-6-Phe-cAMP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing no cAMP increase in the matrix.

claim: Bay 60-7550 is unable to appreciably increase in the matrix the concentration of the membrane permeable cAMP analogue 8-CPT-6-Phe-cAMP.
source: Surprisingly, Bay 60–7550 did not increase cAMP levels in the matrix (Figure 3C) and was unable to appreciably increase in the matrix the concentration of the membrane permeable cAMP analogue 8-CPT-6-Phe-cAMP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No appreciable increase in cAMP is detected in the matrix on inhibition of PDE2A in MEFsPDE2wt expressing matrix-H90.
source: When matrix-H90 was expressed in MEFsPDE2wt no appreciable increase in cAMP was detected in the matrix on inhibition of PDE2A and the response was undistinguishable from that obtained in MEFsPDE2KO expressing the same sensor (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3F showing no cAMP increase in the matrix.

claim: The cAMP response to PDE2A inhibition in the matrix is undistinguishable between MEFsPDE2wt and MEFsPDE2KO.
source: When matrix-H90 was expressed in MEFsPDE2wt no appreciable increase in cAMP was detected in the matrix on inhibition of PDE2A and the response was undistinguishable from that obtained in MEFsPDE2KO expressing the same sensor (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3F showing similar responses in both cell types.

claim: Application of IBMX (100 µM) results in a similar increase in cAMP in the bulk cytosol in MEFsPDE2wt and MEFsPDE2KO.
source: We found that application of IBMX (100 µM) results in a similar increase in cAMP in the bulk cytosol in the two cell types.
evidence: Inferred from FRET measurements comparing the two cell types.

claim: The cAMP increase at the OMM is significantly higher in MEFsPDE2wt than in MEFsPDE2KO upon IBMX treatment.
source: In contrast, the cAMP increase at the OMM is significantly higher in MEFsPDE2wt than in MEFsPDE2KO (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in Figure 3D,E showing differential cAMP increases at the OMM.

claim: No response to Bay 60-7550 is detected in either the cytosol or at the OMM in MEFsPDE2KO.
source: As expected, no response to Bay 60–7550 was detected in either compartment in MEFsPDE2KO.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of PDE2A in knockout cells.

claim: In cardiac myocytes and MEFs, the predominant role of PDE2A is to regulate pmAC-generated cAMP at the OMM.
source: Collectively, the above findings indicate that, at least in cardiac myocytes and MEFs, the predominant role of PDE2A is to regulate pmAC-generated cAMP at the OMM, and that any PDE2A activity in the matrix in these cells is below the detection limit of the matrix-H90 sensor.
evidence: Inferred from the collective FRET imaging data showing cAMP regulation at the OMM but not in the matrix.

claim: Any PDE2A activity in the matrix in cardiac myocytes and MEFs is below the detection limit of the matrix-H90 sensor.
source: Collectively, the above findings indicate that, at least in cardiac myocytes and MEFs, the predominant role of PDE2A is to regulate pmAC-generated cAMP at the OMM, and that any PDE2A activity in the matrix in these cells is below the detection limit of the matrix-H90 sensor.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of detectable cAMP changes in the matrix upon PDE2A inhibition.

claim: PDE2A2 accounts for about 85% of the IBMX-sensitive PDE activity at the OMM.
source: Furthermore, PDE2A2 appears to account for a large fraction (about 85%) of the IBMX-sensitive PDE activity at the OMM.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in cAMP responses between wild-type and PDE2A knockout cells at the OMM.

claim: PDE2A predominantly segregates with the mitochondrial fraction in NRVM.
source: To further investigate the submitochondrial localisation of PDE2A2, we performed western blotting analysis of subcellular fractions from NRVM. PDE2A predominantly segregates with the mitochondrial fraction (Figure 4A) and treatment with proteinase K (PK, 10 µM), which hydrolyses proteins exposed to the cytosolic side of the OMM, significantly reduced the PDE2A signal, although it did not completely ablate it (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing PDE2A in mitochondrial fractions.

claim: Treatment with proteinase K (PK, 10 µM) significantly reduces the PDE2A signal in the mitochondrial fraction but does not completely ablate it.
source: To further investigate the submitochondrial localisation of PDE2A2, we performed western blotting analysis of subcellular fractions from NRVM. PDE2A predominantly segregates with the mitochondrial fraction (Figure 4A) and treatment with proteinase K (PK, 10 µM), which hydrolyses proteins exposed to the cytosolic side of the OMM, significantly reduced the PDE2A signal, although it did not completely ablate it (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing partial reduction of PDE2A signal with proteinase K treatment.

claim: Proteinase K hydrolyses proteins exposed to the cytosolic side of the OMM.
source: To further investigate the submitochondrial localisation of PDE2A2, we performed western blotting analysis of subcellular fractions from NRVM. PDE2A predominantly segregates with the mitochondrial fraction (Figure 4A) and treatment with proteinase K (PK, 10 µM), which hydrolyses proteins exposed to the cytosolic side of the OMM, significantly reduced the PDE2A signal, although it did not completely ablate it (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of proteinase K function in subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: PK treatment completely depletes the mitochondrial fraction of TOM20.
source: As expected, PK treatment completely depleted the mitochondrial fraction of TOM20, a protein exclusively found at the OMM (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing loss of TOM20 signal with PK treatment.

claim: TOM20 is a protein exclusively found at the OMM.
source: As expected, PK treatment completely depleted the mitochondrial fraction of TOM20, a protein exclusively found at the OMM (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TOM20 as an OMM marker.

claim: Endogenous PDE2A is clearly detected in the mitoplast fraction obtained from NRVM.
source: As shown in Figure 4C endogenous PDE2A is clearly detected in the mitoplast fraction obtained from NRVM but is completely depleted on treatment of mitoplasts with PK while with the same treatment the matrix marker COX2 is almost entirely preserved.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing PDE2A in mitoplast fractions.

claim: PDE2A is completely depleted from mitoplasts on treatment with PK.
source: As shown in Figure 4C endogenous PDE2A is clearly detected in the mitoplast fraction obtained from NRVM but is completely depleted on treatment of mitoplasts with PK while with the same treatment the matrix marker COX2 is almost entirely preserved.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing loss of PDE2A signal with PK treatment of mitoplasts.

claim: The matrix marker COX2 is almost entirely preserved on treatment of mitoplasts with PK.
source: As shown in Figure 4C endogenous PDE2A is clearly detected in the mitoplast fraction obtained from NRVM but is completely depleted on treatment of mitoplasts with PK while with the same treatment the matrix marker COX2 is almost entirely preserved.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing preservation of COX2 signal with PK treatment.

claim: PDE2A2 appears to be predominantly located at the periphery of mitochondria and to be excluded from the matrix and from the intra-cristae space.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, PDE2A2 appears to be predominantly located at the periphery of mitochondria and to be excluded from the matrix and from the intra-cristae space (where cytochrome c is mostly found).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data in Figure 4D showing spatial distribution of PDE2A2.

claim: The PDE2A2 signal substantially overlaps with that of the OMM marker TOM20.
source: Our analysis shows that the PDE2A2 signal substantially overlaps with that of the OMM marker TOM20 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing colocalization.

claim: About 7% of immunogold particles localise to the OMM in NRVM.
source: We found that about 7% of the particles localise to the OMM, resulting in a similar number of particles per unit length of membrane at the OMM and IMM.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy immunogold labeling data.

claim: There is a similar number of immunogold particles per unit length of membrane at the OMM and IMM in NRVM.
source: We found that about 7% of the particles localise to the OMM, resulting in a similar number of particles per unit length of membrane at the OMM and IMM.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy immunogold labeling data.

claim: PDE2A2 localises at the OMM and IMM.
source: Overall, the above data support localisation of PDE2A2 at the OMM and IMM, whereas the enzyme appears to be largely excluded from the intra-cristae space and from the matrix.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data from Western blots, STED microscopy, and electron microscopy.

claim: PDE2A2 is largely excluded from the intra-cristae space and from the matrix.
source: Overall, the above data support localisation of PDE2A2 at the OMM and IMM, whereas the enzyme appears to be largely excluded from the intra-cristae space and from the matrix.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data from Western blots, STED microscopy, and electron microscopy.

claim: Mitochondria elongation has been associated with increased mitochondrial membrane potential (△Ψm).
source: Mitochondria elongation has been associated with increased mitochondrial membrane potential (△Ψm) and protection from programmed cell death (Jahani-Asl et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jahani-Asl et al., 2007.

claim: Mitochondria elongation has been associated with protection from programmed cell death.
source: Mitochondria elongation has been associated with increased mitochondrial membrane potential (△Ψm) and protection from programmed cell death (Jahani-Asl et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jahani-Asl et al., 2007.

claim: NRVM pre-treated with Bay 60-7550 have significantly higher △Ψm compared to controls.
source: FCCP application to NRVM loaded with the mitochondrial membrane potential indicator TMRM, revealed a significantly higher △Ψm in myocytes pre-treated with Bay 60–7550 compared to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by TMRM fluorescence data in Figure 5A showing slower decay of membrane potential.

claim: The higher △Ψm on inhibition of PDE2A is not due to accumulation of protons secondary to reduced ATP production.
source: The higher △Ψm on inhibition of PDE2A was not due to accumulation of protons secondary to reduced ATP production, as mitochondrial respiration was not affected by Bay 60–7550 treatment (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements in Figure 5B showing no change in respiration.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is not affected by Bay 60-7550 treatment in NRVM.
source: The higher △Ψm on inhibition of PDE2A was not due to accumulation of protons secondary to reduced ATP production, as mitochondrial respiration was not affected by Bay 60–7550 treatment (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements in Figure 5B.

claim: MEFsPDE2KO are significantly protected from ionomycin-induced cell death compared to MEFswt.
source: We found that, while at the concentration used the two treatments result in comparable death of MEFswt, MEFsPDE2KO are significantly protected from ionomycin- but not staurosporin-induced cell death (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5C showing differential survival.

claim: MEFsPDE2KO are not protected from staurosporin-induced cell death.
source: We found that, while at the concentration used the two treatments result in comparable death of MEFswt, MEFsPDE2KO are significantly protected from ionomycin- but not staurosporin-induced cell death (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5C showing similar death rates.

claim: NRVM treated with Bay 60-7550 are protected from ionomycin-induced cell death.
source: In line with these results, NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 are protected from ionomycin but not staurosporin treatment, an effect that was not observed when the cells were treated with the PDE3 inhibitor cilostamide (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5D showing increased survival.

claim: NRVM treated with Bay 60-7550 are not protected from staurosporin-induced cell death.
source: In line with these results, NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 are protected from ionomycin but not staurosporin treatment, an effect that was not observed when the cells were treated with the PDE3 inhibitor cilostamide (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5D showing no change in survival.

claim: Treatment with the PDE3 inhibitor cilostamide does not protect NRVM from ionomycin or staurosporin treatment.
source: In line with these results, NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 are protected from ionomycin but not staurosporin treatment, an effect that was not observed when the cells were treated with the PDE3 inhibitor cilostamide (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5D showing no protective effect.

claim: Knock down of PDE2A in NRVM by siRNAPDE2 results in a protective effect against ionomycin-induced cell death.
source: Knock down of PDE2A in NRVM by siRNAPDE2 resulted in a similar protective effect (Figure 5E) and there was no difference between ionomycin and staurosporin treatment when the control siRNA sequence 'siglo' was used (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5E showing increased survival with PDE2A knockdown.

claim: There is no difference between ionomycin and staurosporin treatment when the control siRNA sequence 'siglo' is used in NRVM.
source: Knock down of PDE2A in NRVM by siRNAPDE2 resulted in a similar protective effect (Figure 5E) and there was no difference between ionomycin and staurosporin treatment when the control siRNA sequence 'siglo' was used (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data in Figure 5F showing similar death rates.

claim: Treatment with BAY60 completely reverses the effect of ionomycin on △Ψm of NRVM.
source: Treatment with BAY60 also completely reversed the effect of ionomycin on △Ψm of NRVM (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by TMRM fluorescence data in Figure 5G showing preservation of membrane potential.

claim: The number of apoptotic nuclei induced by ionomycin is significantly reduced in NRVM treated with Bay 60-7550.
source: In addition, TUNEL-staining revealed that the number of apoptotic nuclei induced by ionomycin is significantly reduced in NRVM treated with Bay 60–7550 (Figure 5H) compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 5H showing reduced apoptotic nuclei.

claim: MEFsPDE2KO show significantly less TUNEL-positive nuclei upon treatment with ionomycin compared to staurosporin.
source: Furthermore, while MEFsPDE2KO showed significantly less TUNEL-positive nuclei upon treatment with ionomycin compared to staurosporin, MEFswt did not (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 5I showing differential apoptosis.

claim: MEFswt do not show differential TUNEL-positive nuclei between ionomycin and staurosporin treatment.
source: Furthermore, while MEFsPDE2KO showed significantly less TUNEL-positive nuclei upon treatment with ionomycin compared to staurosporin, MEFswt did not (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 5I showing similar apoptosis rates.

claim: Drp1 is required for the anti-apoptotic effect of PDE2A inhibition.
source: We further confirmed the requirement of Drp1 for the anti-apoptotic effect of PDE2A inhibition as application of BAY60 was effective at reducing the number of Tunel-positive nuclei resulting from ionomycin treatment in MEFswt but not in MEFsDrp1KO(Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 5J showing that the protective effect requires Drp1.

claim: Bay 60-7550 treatment results in more elongated mitochondria equally in MEFsWT and MEFssACKO.
source: We found that Bay 60–7550 treatment results in more elongated mitochondria equally in both cell types (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial morphology analysis in Figure 6A showing similar elongation in both cell types.

claim: Pre-treatment with Bay 60-7550 results in a comparable increase in △Ψm in MEFsWT and MEFssACKO.
source: In addition, pre-treatment with Bay 60–7550 resulted in a comparable increase in △Ψm in MEFsWT and MEFssACKO (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by TMRM fluorescence data in Figure 6B showing similar membrane potential increases.

claim: MEFsWT and MEFssACKO are equally resistant to ionomycin treatment.
source: Similarly, TUNEL analysis showed that both cell types were equally resistant to ionomycin treatment and equally sensitive to staurosporin (Figure 6C), confirming that PDE2A2 regulates mitochondria morphology, △Ψm and apoptotic cell death via modulation of cAMP generated by pmAC and not by sAC in the matrix.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 6C showing similar resistance.

claim: MEFsWT and MEFssACKO are equally sensitive to staurosporin.

evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 6C showing similar sensitivity.

claim: cAMP/PKA signalling is compartmentalised with tight spatial and temporal control of signal propagation underpinning specificity of response.
source: cAMP/PKA signalling is compartmentalised with tight spatial and temporal control of signal propagation underpinning specificity of response.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field of cAMP signaling.

claim: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) localise to specific subcellular domains within which they control local cAMP levels.
source: The cAMP-degrading enzymes, phosphodiesterases (PDEs), localise to specific subcellular domains within which they control local cAMP levels and are key regulators of signal compartmentalisation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field of cAMP signaling.

claim: PDEs are key regulators of signal compartmentalisation.
source: The cAMP-degrading enzymes, phosphodiesterases (PDEs), localise to specific subcellular domains within which they control local cAMP levels and are key regulators of signal compartmentalisation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field of cAMP signaling.

claim: Several components of the cAMP/PKA cascade are located to different mitochondrial sub-compartments.
source: Several components of the cAMP/PKA cascade are located to different mitochondrial sub-compartments, suggesting the presence of multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains within the organelle.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field, suggesting multiple signaling domains.

claim: There are multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains within mitochondria.
source: Several components of the cAMP/PKA cascade are located to different mitochondrial sub-compartments, suggesting the presence of multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains within the organelle.
evidence: Inferred from the localization of multiple cAMP/PKA components to different mitochondrial compartments.

claim: Mitochondria produce the majority of ATP required for a cell to function.
source: Mitochondria produce the majority of ATP required for a cell to function and perform vital functions in the maintenance of cellular metabolism and ion homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria perform vital functions in the maintenance of cellular metabolism and ion homeostasis.
source: Mitochondria produce the majority of ATP required for a cell to function and perform vital functions in the maintenance of cellular metabolism and ion homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria play an important role in apoptosis.
source: Additionally, mitochondria play an important role in apoptosis and are implicated in the pathogenesis of many diseases (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012.

claim: Mitochondria are implicated in the pathogenesis of many diseases.
source: Additionally, mitochondria play an important role in apoptosis and are implicated in the pathogenesis of many diseases (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012.

claim: Mitochondria exist in a dynamic network and are continuously remodelled by fusion and fission reactions.
source: Mitochondria exist in a dynamic network and are continuously remodelled by fusion and fission reactions.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Alteration of the fusion/fission balance contributes to the pathogenesis of many complex conditions, including common neurodegenerative diseases, cancers and cardiovascular disorders.
source: Alteration of the fusion/fission balance contributes to the pathogenesis of many complex conditions, including common neurodegenerative diseases, cancers and cardiovascular disorders (Archer, 2013), including the adaptive response to ischaemia–reperfusion injury (Ong et al., 2010; Sharp et al., 2014) and cardiac remodelling associated with heart failure (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Archer, 2013; Ong et al., 2010; Sharp et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Disorganized, small mitochondria are typically found in a variety of cardiac pathologies.
source: Disorganized, small mitochondria are typically found in a variety of cardiac pathologies (Schaper et al., 1991; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schaper et al., 1991 and Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Molecular mediators of mitochondria dynamics are recognised as potential therapeutic targets.
source: As a consequence, molecular mediators of mitochondria dynamics are recognised as potential therapeutic targets (Archer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Archer, 2013.

claim: Mitochondria fission involves dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a GTPase of the dynamin superfamily.
source: Mitochondria fission involves dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a GTPase of the dynamin superfamily, which resides in the cytosol and translocates to the mitochondria upon activation by calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation (Cereghetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cereghetti et al., 2008.

claim: Drp1 resides in the cytosol and translocates to the mitochondria upon activation by calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation.
source: Mitochondria fission involves dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a GTPase of the dynamin superfamily, which resides in the cytosol and translocates to the mitochondria upon activation by calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation (Cereghetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cereghetti et al., 2008.

claim: Drp1 multimerises at the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and is thought to mechanically constrict and eventually sever mitochondria.
source: Drp1 multimerises at the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and is thought to mechanically constrict and eventually sever mitochondria.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drp1 function in mitochondrial fission.

claim: Drp1 is subject to complex post-translational modification by ubiquitylation, sumoylation, nitrosylation and phosphorylation.
source: Drp1 is subject to complex post-translational modification by ubiquitylation, sumoylation, nitrosylation and phosphorylation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drp1 regulation.

claim: Drp1 is inactivated by protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation at serine 637 (ser637), which results in mitochondria elongation.
source: A well-characterised regulation of Drp1 is its inactivation by protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation at serine 637 (ser637), which results in mitochondria elongation (Cereghetti et al., 2008; Cribbs and Strack, 2007; Chang and Blackstone, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cereghetti et al., 2008; Cribbs and Strack, 2007; Chang and Blackstone, 2007.

claim: PKA is a multi-target kinase activated by the ubiquitous second messenger 3',5'-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
source: PKA is a multi-target kinase activated by the ubiquitous second messenger 3',5'-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PKA activation.

claim: cAMP is synthesised either by a plasma membrane-associated adenylyl cyclase (pmAC), upon hormonal activation of Gs protein-coupled receptors, or by a Ca2+ and bicarbonate sensitive soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC).
source: cAMP is synthesised either by a plasma membrane- associated adenylyl cyclase (pmAC), upon hormonal activation of Gs protein-coupled receptors, or by a Ca2+ and bicarbonate sensitive soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC) (Rahman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rahman et al., 2013.

claim: cAMP/PKA signalling regulates fundamental cellular processes, including cell differentiation, growth, metabolism and death.
source: cAMP/PKA signalling regulates fundamental cellular processes, including cell differentiation, growth, metabolism and death (Taskén and Aandahl, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taskén and Aandahl, 2004.

claim: Dysfunctional cAMP signalling has been implicated in multiple disease conditions.
source: Dysfunctional cAMP signalling has been implicated in multiple disease conditions and several drugs currently in use target the cAMP/PKA pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several drugs currently in use target the cAMP/PKA pathway.
source: Dysfunctional cAMP signalling has been implicated in multiple disease conditions and several drugs currently in use target the cAMP/PKA pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: cAMP/PKA signalling is compartmentalised in distinct signalling domains and occurs largely via generation of restricted pools of cAMP that activate PKA subsets tethered in proximity to specific targets via binding to A kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs).
source: cAMP/PKA signalling is compartmentalised in distinct signalling domains and occurs largely via generation of restricted pools of cAMP that activate PKA subsets tethered in proximity to specific targets via binding to A kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) (Langeberg and Scott, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langeberg and Scott, 2015.

claim: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) constitute a superfamily of enzymes, which includes more than 100 isoforms.
source: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) constitute a superfamily of enzymes, which includes more than 100 isoforms, and are the only enzymes that degrade cAMP.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PDE enzymes.

claim: PDEs are the only enzymes that degrade cAMP.
source: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) constitute a superfamily of enzymes, which includes more than 100 isoforms, and are the only enzymes that degrade cAMP.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PDE function.

claim: Different PDE isoforms are uniquely regulated and distributed within the cell.
source: Different PDE isoforms are uniquely regulated and distributed within the cell. Therefore, they differentially determine the local level of cAMP at specific subcellular sites, dictating which PKA targets are phosphorylated and the specificity of the downstream response (Maurice et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maurice et al., 2014.

claim: PDE isoforms differentially determine the local level of cAMP at specific subcellular sites, dictating which PKA targets are phosphorylated and the specificity of the downstream response.
source: Different PDE isoforms are uniquely regulated and distributed within the cell. Therefore, they differentially determine the local level of cAMP at specific subcellular sites, dictating which PKA targets are phosphorylated and the specificity of the downstream response (Maurice et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maurice et al., 2014.

claim: A number of components of the cAMP signalling cascade have been located at the mitochondria, including multiple AKAPs and PDEs.
source: A number of components of the cAMP signalling cascade have been located at the mitochondria, including multiple AKAPs (Huang et al., 1999; Alto et al., 2002; Means et al., 2011) and PDEs (Cercek and Houslay, 1982; Shimizu-Albergine et al., 2012; Acin-Perez et al., 2011), suggesting the co-existence at the organelle of multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains (Lefkimmiatis and Zaccolo, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 1999; Alto et al., 2002; Means et al., 2011; Cercek and Houslay, 1982; Shimizu-Albergine et al., 2012; Acin-Perez et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains co-exist at the mitochondria.
source: A number of components of the cAMP signalling cascade have been located at the mitochondria, including multiple AKAPs (Huang et al., 1999; Alto et al., 2002; Means et al., 2011) and PDEs (Cercek and Houslay, 1982; Shimizu-Albergine et al., 2012; Acin-Perez et al., 2011), suggesting the co-existence at the organelle of multiple cAMP/PKA signalling domains (Lefkimmiatis and Zaccolo, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the localization of multiple cAMP signaling components to mitochondria, with citation to Lefkimmiatis and Zaccolo, 2014.

claim: PDE2A is a 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)-activated PDE that degrades both cAMP and cGMP.
source: PDE2A is a 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)-activated PDE that degrades both cAMP and cGMP (Stroop and Beavo, 1991) and is expressed in a number of tissues, including brain, heart, liver, lung, adipose tissue and adrenal gland.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stroop and Beavo, 1991.

claim: PDE2A is expressed in a number of tissues, including brain, heart, liver, lung, adipose tissue and adrenal gland.
source: PDE2A is a 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)-activated PDE that degrades both cAMP and cGMP (Stroop and Beavo, 1991) and is expressed in a number of tissues, including brain, heart, liver, lung, adipose tissue and adrenal gland.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PDE2A expression.

claim: Three variants of the Pde2a gene are expressed (PDE2A1, PDE2A2 and PDE2A3).
source: Three variants of the Pde2a gene are expressed (PDE2A1, PDE2A2 and PDE2A3). The variants differ in their amino termini, and this variation may explain their different subcellular localisations (Lugnier, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lugnier, 2006.

claim: The PDE2A variants differ in their amino termini, and this variation may explain their different subcellular localisations.
source: Three variants of the Pde2a gene are expressed (PDE2A1, PDE2A2 and PDE2A3). The variants differ in their amino termini, and this variation may explain their different subcellular localisations (Lugnier, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lugnier, 2006.

claim: Genetic ablation of PDE2A results in high embryonic lethality past E17.5–E18.5 dpc.
source: Genetic ablation of PDE2A results in high embryonic lethality past E17.5–E18.5 dpc (Stephenson et al., 2009), indicating that these enzymes are involved in vital biological functions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephenson et al., 2009.

claim: PDE2A enzymes are involved in vital biological functions.
source: Genetic ablation of PDE2A results in high embryonic lethality past E17.5–E18.5 dpc (Stephenson et al., 2009), indicating that these enzymes are involved in vital biological functions.
evidence: Inferred from the high embryonic lethality observed in PDE2A knockout mice.

claim: PDE2A2 localisation at mitochondrial membranes is not homogeneous but shows a dotted appearance.
source: Our STED analysis shows that PDE2A2 localisation at mitochondrial membranes is not homogeneous but shows a dotted appearance (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which suggests that PDE2A2 may be part of a protein cluster (Jans et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PDE2A2 may be part of a protein cluster at mitochondrial membranes.
source: Our STED analysis shows that PDE2A2 localisation at mitochondrial membranes is not homogeneous but shows a dotted appearance (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which suggests that PDE2A2 may be part of a protein cluster (Jans et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the dotted appearance in STED images, with citation to Jans et al., 2013.

claim: Numerous studies have linked PDE2A to pathological conditions, including psychiatric, neurological, cardiovascular and respiratory disorders.
source: Numerous studies have linked PDE2A to pathological conditions, including psychiatric, neurological (Xu et al., 2015), cardiovascular (Mehel et al., 2013), (Li et al., 2015) and respiratory (Zhang et al., 2015) disorders.
evidence: Supported by citations to Xu et al., 2015; Mehel et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in a number of conditions, such as cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), pulmonary hypertension (Bubb et al., 2014) as well as depression, anxiety and cognition deficits in Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zoccarato et al., 2015.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in pulmonary hypertension.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in a number of conditions, such as cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), pulmonary hypertension (Bubb et al., 2014) as well as depression, anxiety and cognition deficits in Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bubb et al., 2014.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in depression, anxiety and cognition deficits in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of PDE2A in animal models has been shown to have beneficial effects in a number of conditions, such as cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), pulmonary hypertension (Bubb et al., 2014) as well as depression, anxiety and cognition deficits in Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: A phase I clinical trial examining a PDE2A inhibitor for the treatment of schizophrenia is currently ongoing.
source: A phase I clinical trial examining a PDE2A inhibitor for the treatment of schizophrenia is currently ongoing (Takeda, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takeda, 2015.

claim: The positive effect of PDE2A inhibitors on depression/anxiety-like behaviours has been linked to their anti-apoptotic effects.
source: The positive effect of PDE2A inhibitors on depression/anxiety-like behaviours has been linked to their anti-apoptotic effects (Ding et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of Drp1 was shown to preserve mitochondria morphology and to prevent cell death in a model of myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury.
source: In addition, inhibition of Drp1 was shown to preserve mitochondria morphology and to prevent cell death in a model of myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (Sharp et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp et al., 2014.

claim: Increased PDE2A expression was reported both in rodents and in human heart failure.
source: Increased PDE2A expression was reported both in rodents (Hua et al., 2012) and in human (Aye et al., 2012) heart failure and PDE2A inhibition was shown to reduce cardiac hypertrophic remodelling in a mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), indicating that PDE2A inhibition may be of therapeutic value in this context.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hua et al., 2012 and Aye et al., 2012.

claim: PDE2A inhibition was shown to reduce cardiac hypertrophic remodelling in a mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Increased PDE2A expression was reported both in rodents (Hua et al., 2012) and in human (Aye et al., 2012) heart failure and PDE2A inhibition was shown to reduce cardiac hypertrophic remodelling in a mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), indicating that PDE2A inhibition may be of therapeutic value in this context.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zoccarato et al., 2015.

claim: PDE2A inhibition may be of therapeutic value in heart failure.
source: Increased PDE2A expression was reported both in rodents (Hua et al., 2012) and in human (Aye et al., 2012) heart failure and PDE2A inhibition was shown to reduce cardiac hypertrophic remodelling in a mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy (Zoccarato et al., 2015), indicating that PDE2A inhibition may be of therapeutic value in this context.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PDE2A inhibition reduces cardiac hypertrophic remodeling.

claim: Knock down of the mitochondrial fusion protein mitofusin 2, which results in fragmented mitochondria, also leads to cardiac myocyte hypertrophy.
source: However, it is interesting to note that knock down of the mitochondrial fusion protein mitofusin 2, which results in fragmented mitochondria, also leads to cardiac myocyte hypertrophy, suggesting a possible direct link between mitochondria fragmentation and cardiac myocytes hypertrophic growth (Pennanen et al., 2014; Guan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pennanen et al., 2014 and Guan et al., 2016.

claim: There may be a direct link between mitochondria fragmentation and cardiac myocytes hypertrophic growth.
source: However, it is interesting to note that knock down of the mitochondrial fusion protein mitofusin 2, which results in fragmented mitochondria, also leads to cardiac myocyte hypertrophy, suggesting a possible direct link between mitochondria fragmentation and cardiac myocytes hypertrophic growth (Pennanen et al., 2014; Guan et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mitochondrial fragmentation is associated with cardiac hypertrophy, with citations to Pennanen et al., 2014 and Guan et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibition of PDE2A2, by enhancing the hormone-dependent cAMP response locally, affects mitochondria dynamics.
source: We further demonstrate that inhibition of PDE2A, by enhancing the hormone-dependent cAMP response locally, affects mitochondria dynamics and protects from apoptotic cell death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial elongation and protection from apoptosis.

claim: Inhibition of PDE2A protects from apoptotic cell death.
source: We further demonstrate that inhibition of PDE2A, by enhancing the hormone-dependent cAMP response locally, affects mitochondria dynamics and protects from apoptotic cell death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced apoptosis with PDE2A inhibition.

claim: In rat cardiac myocytes and other cell types mitochondrial PDE2A2 regulates local cAMP levels.
source: Using pharmacological and genetic approaches combined with real-time FRET imaging and high resolution microscopy, we demonstrate that in rat cardiac myocytes and other cell types mitochondrial PDE2A2 regulates local cAMP levels and PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing cAMP regulation at mitochondria.

claim: In rat cardiac myocytes and other cell types mitochondrial PDE2A2 regulates PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
source: Using pharmacological and genetic approaches combined with real-time FRET imaging and high resolution microscopy, we demonstrate that in rat cardiac myocytes and other cell types mitochondrial PDE2A2 regulates local cAMP levels and PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased Drp1 phosphorylation with PDE2A inhibition.

claim: PDE2A2 is part of a novel cAMP/PKA signalling domain localised at mitochondrial membranes.
source: Here, we describe a novel cAMP/PKA signalling domain localised at mitochondrial membranes and regulated by PDE2A2.
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data showing PDE2A2 localization and function at mitochondrial membranes.

claim: This novel cAMP/PKA signalling domain at mitochondrial membranes is regulated by PDE2A2.
source: Here, we describe a novel cAMP/PKA signalling domain localised at mitochondrial membranes and regulated by PDE2A2.
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data showing PDE2A2 regulation of cAMP and PKA activity at mitochondria.

claim: In cardiac myocytes and other cell types PDE2A2 is part of a distinct cAMP/PKA signalling domain located at the mitochondria but outside the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in cardiac myocytes and other cell types PDE2A2 is part of a distinct cAMP/PKA signalling domain located at the mitochondria but outside the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation, FRET imaging, and microscopy data showing PDE2A2 at mitochondrial membranes but not in the matrix.

claim: This PDE2A2 subset localises to mitochondrial membranes where it controls a pool of cAMP generated at the plasma membrane by the hormone-responsive pmAC.
source: This PDE2A2 subset localises to mitochondrial membranes where it controls a pool of cAMP generated at the plasma membrane by the hormone-responsive pmAC, and regulates PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing that PDE2A2 regulates pmAC-generated cAMP at the OMM, and experiments with sAC knockout cells.

claim: PDE2A2 at mitochondrial membranes regulates PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
source: This PDE2A2 subset localises to mitochondrial membranes where it controls a pool of cAMP generated at the plasma membrane by the hormone-responsive pmAC, and regulates PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Drp1.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased Drp1 phosphorylation with PDE2A inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of PDE2A2 at mitochondrial membranes results in elongated mitochondria.
source: Inhibition of this subset of PDE2A2 results in elongated mitochondria and protection from mitochondrial-dependent cell death.
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial morphology analysis showing elongation with PDE2A inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of PDE2A2 at mitochondrial membranes results in protection from mitochondrial-dependent cell death.
source: Inhibition of this subset of PDE2A2 results in elongated mitochondria and protection from mitochondrial-dependent cell death.
evidence: Supported by cell viability and TUNEL assay data showing protection from ionomycin-induced apoptosis.
